content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Understanding Solana Accounts
Understanding Solana Accounts
Accounts are Solana's primary storage primitives. They hold data, a lamport balance, and an owner program. This model powers high-performance programs and clear permission boundaries.
In this lesson
You will learn the account model, ownership rules, rent, and keypair CLI commands so you can create and manage accounts on devnet.
Why it matters
The account model determines how programs control state, how persistence is funded, and how wallets map to on-chain storage. Good account design prevents data loss and bugs.
Explore Key Topics
Account Model
Accounts store data, have an owner program, and a lamport balance.
Ownership & Security
Only the owning program can modify an account's data — a key permission concept.
Rent & CLI
Rent-exemption and solana-keygen commands ensure persistence and developer control.
Interactive Concept
Account
address = public key; owner = program; data & lamports
Keypair
public key derived from a keypair; private key signs transactions
Rent
small lamport deposit required for storage; rent-exempt if threshold met
Quick glance
Treat accounts as addressable files. Their owner program controls updates. Keep private keys secure and make accounts rent-exempt when you need persistent state. Use CLI to create and fund devnet accounts for testing.

screens.title: What is a Solana Account?
screens.narratorSegment: A Solana account is best thought of as a small addressable file on a distributed ledger. It has a public key that serves as its address, a balance measured in lamports that pays for storage, a data field that holds arbitrary bytes, and an owner program that controls how that data may change. This contrasts with wallet-centric models where accounts are primarily keys tied to balances. On Solana, even program code lives in a program account, and application state is stored in data accounts. For example, an NFT's metadata and ownership can live in a data account whose owner is the NFT program. The owner field is crucial: only the owning program may modify the account's data, so ownership enforces permissions at the protocol level. A common misconception is to think that the private key alone changes data; while a private key signs transactions, the program logic — guided by ownership — dictates whether those signed transactions can modify a given account. Key takeaways: treat accounts as the source of truth for application state, always note the owner when designing your program, and remember that lamports fund persistence. How does this view change your mental model of wallet versus state?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Account = addressable storage + owner program + data + lamport balance; ownership enforces who may change data.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › What is a Solana Account?
Definition & components
  • Address: a public key uniquely identifying the account.
  • Owner: the program that may modify the account's data.
  • Lamports: a small SOL balance used to pay for storage and determine rent-exemption.
  • Data: arbitrary bytes storing application state, metadata, or executable code.
Concrete example
An NFT uses a data account to store metadata. The NFT program owns that account. Only the NFT program can update the metadata field, and lamports ensure the account remains stored if rent-exempt.
Key Takeaway

Think of accounts as files: the owner program controls edits, lamports pay for storage, and public keys name the files.

Annotated structure
Public Key
Unique address; derived from a keypair.
Owner Program
Only this program may modify the data bytes.
Lamports
Funds stored to pay rent and enable persistence.
Data
Application bytes: balances, metadata, or executable code.
Common misconception
Some learners assume private keys alone change state. In fact, signatures authenticate the transaction, but ownership and program logic determine whether an account's data is changed. Signing is necessary but not sufficient.

screens.title: Account Types: System, Program, Data
screens.narratorSegment: Solana classifies accounts by role: system accounts, program accounts, and data accounts. System accounts are owned by the Solana System Program and handle native SOL transfers and basic account creation. Program accounts store executable program code and are marked as executable; they are loaded and invoked by the runtime. Data accounts hold application state like token balances or metadata and are owned by the program responsible for managing that state. Consider a token wallet: the token balance lives in a data account owned by the SPL Token Program. The SPL token program is distinct from the System Program; the former defines token rules while the latter handles raw SOL. A useful comparison: system accounts handle core ledger primitives, program accounts contain business logic code, and data accounts store that logic's state. A common beginner error is treating all accounts interchangeably — if you try to write state from a program that isn't the account owner, the runtime will reject the change. Concrete example: to update a user's token balance, the token program must be the account owner and receive that account as a writable parameter in the instruction. Key takeaway: design which program will own each account before you allocate storage.

Key Takeaway

screens.title: Ownership: How Programs Interact with Accounts
screens.narratorSegment: Ownership is the mechanism that tells the runtime which program can modify an account's data. When submitting an instruction, you explicitly pass the accounts the program will read or write. The runtime checks that any attempted write is permitted: the target account must be marked writable in the transaction and it must be owned by the invoked program. For example, if a token program needs to debit a token balance, the token account must be passed as a writable argument and must be owned by the SPL Token Program. If it is not owned by that program, the runtime will prevent the write. Ownership also simplifies security reasoning: ownership decouples who can sign a transaction from who can change data. A private key holder can sign to authenticate actions, but without the correct account ownership and instruction parameters, the program cannot alter the account bytes. A common error is forgetting to pass the account as writable or passing the wrong owner; both produce runtime errors. Practice: when designing an instruction, list every account it needs, mark read/write appropriately, and ensure ownership aligns with the intended program. This prevents permission errors before runtime.

keyIdea.title: Ownership rule
keyIdea.text: A program may modify an account only if that account is passed to the instruction, marked writable, and owned by the program.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Ownership: Program Interaction
Ownership flow
  1. Design instruction: list required accounts and whether each is writable.
  2. Invoke program: pass accounts as parameters to the instruction.
  3. Runtime checks: verifies ownership and writable flags before applying writes.
  4. Program executes: only permitted accounts are modified by program logic.
Concrete example
A token transfer instruction must receive the sender and receiver token accounts as parameters. The SPL Token Program must own those accounts and the sender account must be writable to debit the balance; otherwise the transfer fails at runtime.
Architecture callouts
Signer vs Owner
Signing proves intent. Ownership grants permission to mutate data. Both are required in correct combinations.
Writable flag
Always mark accounts you expect the program to mutate as writable in the instruction to avoid runtime rejections.
Common mistake
Forgetting to pass an account as writable or passing a differently owned account are common causes of failed instructions. Verify account owners and flags when debugging.

screens.title: Keypairs, Public Keys, and Private Keys
screens.narratorSegment: A keypair consists of a public key and a private key. The public key is the account's address on Solana; the private key is the secret used to sign transactions, proving control over the account. Generating a keypair produces a new public address you can use to receive funds or create accounts. Importantly, the private key should remain secret: anyone with access can sign transactions and transfer funds or modify accounts that accept signatures from that key. A persistent beginner mistake is committing private key files to public repositories. For development, use separate devnet keys and always protect mainnet keys by storing them offline or encrypting them with a strong passphrase. Practically, the CLI workflow goes: generate a keypair file, derive the public key from it, then check the balance of that public key. In the next screens we'll show the exact solana-keygen commands. For now, remember the conceptual map: keypair generates an address; the public key is for others to send you SOL, and the private key signs transactions that move funds or interact with programs. Ending question: where will you store your private keys while developing?

keyIdea.text: Public key = account address; private key = secret used to sign transactions and control that address.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Keypairs & Keys
Concept cards
Keypair
Generates a public and private key. The public key becomes an account address.
Public key
Address others use to send SOL. Safe to share.
Private key
Secret used to sign. Must be kept secure and encrypted for real funds.
Security note
Use passphrase encryption for key files and separate devnet keys from mainnet keys. Treat private keys like bank account credentials.
Analogy
Think of the public key as your mailbox number and the private key as the key that opens the mailbox. Anyone can drop mail into the box but only the holder of the private key can take mail out.
Example scenario
After generating a keypair file, you run a command to show the public key, then request an airdrop to that public key on devnet so you can test transactions without real funds.

screens.title: CLI Walkthrough: Generate a Keypair
screens.narratorSegment: Now let's walk through creating a new keypair with the CLI. The standard developer flow is to run the key-generation command which outputs a keypair file on disk and a public key you can use as an address. In practice you will be prompted to set a passphrase; it's recommended to use one for any key that could touch real funds. The example command generates a file named my-keypair. json and prints the public key to the terminal. After generation, you'll derive the public key from the file and verify its balance. A common beginner step is to forget to secure the file; always encrypt or move it to safe storage. For development, keep a separate devnet key and use its public key when requesting an airdrop. This screen shows the exact command snippet and example output so you can copy it into a terminal later. Remember: generating a keypair creates a new potential account address, but it does not yet fund the account; balance will be zero until you add lamports. CLI Walkthrough: Generate a Keypair means generate a keypair file with solana-keygen, set a passphrase, then derive the public key for later use.. In practical terms, using solana-keygen to create a new keypair file. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Command (example)
# Generate a new keypair and save it to 'my-keypair.json'

# Example output:
# Generating a new keypair

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Derive & Check Balance
Commands (examples)
# Get the public key from a keypair file
solana-keygen pubkey my-keypair.json

# Check the balance of that public key
solana balance $(solana-keygen pubkey my-keypair.json)

# On devnet, include --url devnet when necessary
you can also run: solana balance  --url devnet
Example output
A newly generated account typically shows 0 SOL. After an airdrop it will show the funded amount, which confirms the account holds lamports.
Checklist before airdrop
  • Copy the printed public key to avoid typos.
  • Confirm your CLI is pointed to devnet if you intend to use devnet.
  • Verify the balance is zero before requesting test funds.
Key Takeaway
Always confirm addresses and networks before funding. Mistargeted airdrops go to the wrong public key and are hard to recover.

screens.title: Activity: Create and Fund a Devnet Account
screens.narratorSegment: This activity walks you through creating and funding a devnet account step by step. First, generate a keypair file and set a passphrase for security. Second, derive the public key from the file and copy it. Third, confirm the initial balance is zero. Fourth, request a devnet airdrop of one SOL to that public key and finally re-check the balance to confirm funding. Each step is essential: generating without securing the file risks exposure, copying the wrong public key wastes an airdrop, and checking the balance before-and-after validates that funds arrived. A recommended habit is to name test key files clearly, such as devnet-wallet. json, and to keep them encrypted. Also, always include --url devnet when in doubt so you don't accidentally operate against mainnet. This exercise helps you internalize the CLI flow and gives you a funded test address for subsequent lessons where you'll interact with programs and accounts. Step-by-step commands

This simple flow gets you a funded devnet account so you can experiment safely without mainnet funds.

screens.title: Rent and Rent-Exemption
screens.narratorSegment: Solana requires accounts to hold lamports to pay for storage. If an account's balance is too low for its data size, the network may deallocate it to reclaim space. This mechanism prevents unbounded state growth. To persist data indefinitely, you deposit enough lamports to reach the rent-exempt threshold for the account size. The threshold depends on data length; larger accounts need more lamports. Most SDKs and program builders calculate this amount for you when creating accounts, but it's important to understand why the deposit exists and what happens if it's missing. For example, a small state account can be made rent-exempt so that the program doesn't need to pay recurring rent. A common misunderstanding is thinking rent-exemption is a monthly fee; instead it's a one-time deposit that secures the account's storage. If you later shrink or expand account data, re-evaluate rent-exemption. In practice, when designing a dApp, prefer making critical state accounts rent-exempt to avoid accidental deallocation and data loss. Ask yourself: which accounts in your app require permanent persistence? content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Rent & Rent-Exemption
Why rent exists
Rent prevents unlimited on-chain storage by requiring a lamport deposit that corresponds to the account's size. Without sufficient balance, accounts can be reclaimed.
Rent-exempt deposit
If an account holds the required amount for its size, it becomes rent-exempt and will persist indefinitely without recurring charges. SDKs typically compute this amount for you.
Concrete guidance
  • Estimate account size before creating it so you can compute rent-exempt balance.
  • Make critical state accounts rent-exempt to avoid accidental deallocation.
  • When modifying data size, re-check rent-exemption and top up if necessary.
Key Takeaway
Treat rent-exemption as a one-time storage deposit that guarantees persistence. Plan deposits based on account size.

screens.title: Security & Common Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Security in account management centers around two concerns: private key safety and correct storage funding. Private keys sign transactions and therefore control accounts. Common mistakes include committing keypair files to a public repository or reusing a keypair for both development and production. Use separate devnet keys and encrypt files with a passphrase for anything beyond throwaway tests. For storage funding, failing to make critical accounts rent-exempt can lead to deallocation and lost state. When debugging missing state, first check the account's balance and whether it met the rent-exempt threshold. Another frequent error is misassigning account ownership, which leads to runtime failures when the invoked program attempts writes. Finally, always validate the account list passed to an instruction: ensure required writable accounts are present and owners match the program logic. Following these practices will reduce accidental losses and runtime errors. Ask yourself: which of your project's accounts need rent-exemption and which keys must remain offline? fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we explore what an account is on Solana and why that model matters. Unlike some platforms where accounts are mainly wallet containers, Solana treats every piece of persistent state as an account — a small, addressable file identified by a public key, owned by a program, and holding data and lamports. You'll learn the three common account roles — system, program, and data — and how ownership controls who can change an account's contents. We'll also cover rent and rent-exemption, a storage funding rule that determines whether an account persists. Finally, you'll see practical CLI steps: generating a keypair, deriving its public key, checking balance, and funding a devnet account with an airdrop. Understanding these fundamentals helps you design accounts for dApps, avoid persistent storage mistakes, and manage key security. As you go through the lessons, keep in mind a mental model: an account is a storage container with an owner program and a small balance that pays for its persistence. That model drives how programs interact with state and how you structure your application.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain Solana's account model in practical terms: what an account stores, how an account is identified, and why ownership matters. You will distinguish system accounts, program accounts, and data accounts and give an example of each. You will understand how a program becomes the owner of an account and how ownership enforces who can modify an account's data. You will also be able to describe rent and rent exemption — how a lamport balance funds storage and why making an account rent-exempt ensures persistence. Finally, you'll learn the CLI basics to generate a keypair and check an account's balance so you can create and fund a devnet test account. These skills let you manage state safely and diagnose why accounts might be deallocated or remain unchanged. As you practice, remember that private keys grant control, and ownership is the on-chain permission that programs respect.

This page focuses on hands-on skills and safety practices. You will learn to generate new keypairs using the CLI, derive a public key for that pair, and verify an account balance on devnet. You'll practice requesting an airdrop for development and confirm the funding step. Equally important is private key safety: you'll learn why private keys must be kept offline or encrypted and why committing keys to public repositories is dangerous. We'll cover a common beginner mistake — exposing private keys — and a mitigation pattern: use passphrase encryption and devnet-only keys for experiments. These skills let you prototype confidently, reproduce issues, and keep test funds and real funds separate. As you practice, remember to treat private keys like the secret keys to a bank account and never share them. By the end you should be able to both execute the CLI steps and explain why each step is necessary and safe.

A Solana account is best thought of as a small addressable file on a distributed ledger. It has a public key that serves as its address, a balance measured in lamports that pays for storage, a data field that holds arbitrary bytes, and an owner program that controls how that data may change. This contrasts with wallet-centric models where accounts are primarily keys tied to balances. On Solana, even program code lives in a program account, and application state is stored in data accounts. For example, an NFT's metadata and ownership can live in a data account whose owner is the NFT program. The owner field is crucial: only the owning program may modify the account's data, so ownership enforces permissions at the protocol level. A common misconception is to think that the private key alone changes data; while a private key signs transactions, the program logic — guided by ownership — dictates whether those signed transactions can modify a given account. Key takeaways: treat accounts as the source of truth for application state, always note the owner when designing your program, and remember that lamports fund persistence. How does this view change your mental model of wallet versus state?

Solana classifies accounts by role: system accounts, program accounts, and data accounts. System accounts are owned by the Solana System Program and handle native SOL transfers and basic account creation. Program accounts store executable program code and are marked as executable; they are loaded and invoked by the runtime. Data accounts hold application state like token balances or metadata and are owned by the program responsible for managing that state. Consider a token wallet: the token balance lives in a data account owned by the SPL Token Program. The SPL token program is distinct from the System Program; the former defines token rules while the latter handles raw SOL. A useful comparison: system accounts handle core ledger primitives, program accounts contain business logic code, and data accounts store that logic's state. A common beginner error is treating all accounts interchangeably — if you try to write state from a program that isn't the account owner, the runtime will reject the change. Concrete example: to update a user's token balance, the token program must be the account owner and receive that account as a writable parameter in the instruction. Key takeaway: design which program will own each account before you allocate storage.

Ownership is the mechanism that tells the runtime which program can modify an account's data. When submitting an instruction, you explicitly pass the accounts the program will read or write. The runtime checks that any attempted write is permitted: the target account must be marked writable in the transaction and it must be owned by the invoked program. For example, if a token program needs to debit a token balance, the token account must be passed as a writable argument and must be owned by the SPL Token Program. If it is not owned by that program, the runtime will prevent the write. Ownership also simplifies security reasoning: ownership decouples who can sign a transaction from who can change data. A private key holder can sign to authenticate actions, but without the correct account ownership and instruction parameters, the program cannot alter the account bytes. A common error is forgetting to pass the account as writable or passing the wrong owner; both produce runtime errors. Practice: when designing an instruction, list every account it needs, mark read/write appropriately, and ensure ownership aligns with the intended program. This prevents permission errors before runtime.

A keypair consists of a public key and a private key. The public key is the account's address on Solana; the private key is the secret used to sign transactions, proving control over the account. Generating a keypair produces a new public address you can use to receive funds or create accounts. Importantly, the private key should remain secret: anyone with access can sign transactions and transfer funds or modify accounts that accept signatures from that key. A persistent beginner mistake is committing private key files to public repositories. For development, use separate devnet keys and always protect mainnet keys by storing them offline or encrypting them with a strong passphrase. Practically, the CLI workflow goes: generate a keypair file, derive the public key from it, then check the balance of that public key. In the next screens we'll show the exact solana-keygen commands. For now, remember the conceptual map: keypair generates an address; the public key is for others to send you SOL, and the private key signs transactions that move funds or interact with programs. Ending question: where will you store your private keys while developing?

Now let's walk through creating a new keypair with the CLI. The standard developer flow is to run the key-generation command which outputs a keypair file on disk and a public key you can use as an address. In practice you will be prompted to set a passphrase; it's recommended to use one for any key that could touch real funds. The example command generates a file named my-keypair. json and prints the public key to the terminal. After generation, you'll derive the public key from the file and verify its balance. A common beginner step is to forget to secure the file; always encrypt or move it to safe storage. For development, keep a separate devnet key and use its public key when requesting an airdrop. This screen shows the exact command snippet and example output so you can copy it into a terminal later. Remember: generating a keypair creates a new potential account address, but it does not yet fund the account; balance will be zero until you add lamports.
